# **Exhaustive Analysis of Regression Language Models for Code: Dataset Validity, Methodological Critique, and Experimental Verification**

## **Executive Overview of Code-to-Metric Regression and Performance Prediction**

The paradigm of predicting the physical or systemic outcomes of executing source code—frequently termed performance prediction, static analysis, or code-to-metric regression—has historically been an intensely studied domain within systems engineering, compiler optimization, and hardware-software co-design.1 Historically, this domain has been dominated by heavy, domain-specific feature engineering. Traditional analytical methods have relied on parsing Abstract Syntax Trees (ASTs), compiling intermediate representations (IR), or engineering topological structures for processing via Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to map source code to numeric performance indicators like memory footprint, execution latency, or neural network accuracy.1 While effective within narrow, highly constrained environments, these legacy methodologies possess severe rigidities. They require bespoke parsing logic for every new programming language, and their underlying models struggle to generalize across diverse hardware platforms without retraining on completely novel topological structures.  
The research paper titled "Regression Language Models for Code" (arXiv:2509.26476) introduces a radical departure from these established algorithmic norms.1 By framing regression as a sequence-to-sequence translation task, the authors propose that a unified Regression Language Model (RLM) can directly ingest raw source code text and output precise numeric predictions, circumventing the need for specialized data structures, ASTs, or IR compilations entirely.4 The authors assert that an RLM, leveraging a frozen language model encoder, can simultaneously predict the memory footprint of Python and C++ code, the latency of Triton GPU kernels, and the accuracy of trained neural networks represented in the Open Neural Network Exchange (ONNX) format, all directly from unstructured text.3  
This analysis provides a comprehensive, multi-dimensional examination of the RLM framework, coupled with an exhaustive academic critique of the methodology presented in the paper, utilizing insights from peer reviews and independent empirical diagnostics. Furthermore, in direct alignment with the requirement to deeply assess the accompanying dataset—available via the Hugging Face repository akhauriyash/Code-Regression—this report outlines a rigorous, non-neural experimental framework.7 This framework is specifically designed to validate the dataset's statistical integrity, structural coherence, and baseline suitability for regression modeling without necessitating the training, fine-tuning, or inference of any Large Language Models (LLMs). By systematically dissecting the dataset's overarching schema, its constituent sub-corpora (APPS, CDSS, and KBSS), and the underlying statistical variance of its target variables, the subsequent sections offer a foundational blueprint for evaluating the data's raw predictive signal using classical machine learning and rigorous statistical diagnostics.

## **Theoretical Foundations of the Regression Language Model Architecture**

To effectively critique the paper and objectively evaluate its accompanying training data, one must first deconstruct the theoretical mechanics of the Regression Language Model itself. The core innovation of the paper lies not in the proposition of a novel transformer architecture, but rather in a reimagined formulation of the regression objective function, continuous target tokenization, and multi-objective decoding.8

### **Sequence-to-Sequence Numerical Tokenization**

Traditional neural regression architectures, such as Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) or classical Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), function by mapping high-dimensional latent states to continuous scalar values using a linear projection head. These models are almost exclusively optimized via geometric distance metrics, such as Mean Squared Error (MSE), Mean Absolute Error (MAE), or Huber loss. The authors of the RLM paper categorically discard this approach.8 Instead, they formulate regression as a conditional maximum likelihood estimation problem, treating continuous numbers purely as text strings generated by an autoregressive decoder.4  
The model leverages a standard encoder-decoder architecture. Specifically, the authors utilize a frozen T5Gemma pretrained encoder to process the input strings. By freezing the encoder, they significantly reduce the computational cost of performing backward passes during training, while simultaneously utilizing the encoder's well-calibrated pretrained linguistic knowledge to map the syntax of the code.3 The decoder is a standard transformer decoder initialized from scratch.10  
The critical mechanism enabling this architecture is the tokenization of the continuous target metrics (e.g., latency, memory). Rather than outputting a single scalar activation, the targets are tokenized explicitly into a specialized digit-by-digit format comprising a sign, a mantissa, and an exponent. According to the experimental setups documented in the research, the tokenizer utilizes a digit base of ![][image1], an exponent length of ![][image2], and a mantissa length of ![][image3].10 For example, a target value of 72.5 might be serialized into discrete vocabulary tokens as \<+\>\<E\>.9

### **Cross-Entropy Optimization for Continuous Targets**

By tokenizing the numeric targets, the model can learn by minimizing the cross-entropy loss over the vocabulary of digit tokens rather than computing Euclidean distances between continuous scalars.8 The authors argue that this token-level cross-entropy loss is vastly superior for multi-task regression.8 In traditional multi-task setups optimized via MSE, catastrophic scaling imbalances occur when attempting to combine tasks with vastly different numerical ranges into a single loss function—for instance, balancing the prediction of memory usage in billions of bytes against execution latency measured in fractions of a millisecond. Cross-entropy normalizes this optimization because the model is simply predicting the next most probable categorical token from the numeric vocabulary, insulating the gradients from exponential magnitude explosions.8  
Furthermore, the paper highlights that the autoregressive nature of the transformer decoder permits the conditional modeling of multiple objectives simultaneously. By consecutively decoding more numbers, the model inherently models the joint probability ![][image4], which naturally captures the inherent physical constraints and trade-offs between interconnected execution metrics, such as the trade-off between algorithmic accuracy and hardware latency.3

### **Empirical Performance Assertions**

Empirically, the authors claim highly robust performance utilizing relatively compact models. They state that a 300 million parameter RLM achieves a Spearman-rank correlation (![][image5]) exceeding 0.90 on memory footprint predictions for Python competitive programming submissions within the APPS dataset.1 Furthermore, they assert that a single, unified model achieves an average Spearman-rank correlation of ![][image6] across 17 distinct programming languages present in the CodeNet corpus.1 In the domain of Neural Architecture Search (NAS), the RLM purportedly achieves an average Kendall-Tau (![][image7]) of 0.46 across five classic NAS design spaces (including NDS, NB-101, NB-201, FBNet, and Ofa-MB) which were previously dominated by highly specialized graph neural networks.3

## **Anatomical Dissection of the Code-Regression Dataset**

The empirical claims of the RLM framework are anchored entirely by the data collated in the akhauriyash/Code-Regression dataset. Understanding the deep structural idiosyncrasies, schema anomalies, and subset distributions of this dataset is absolutely paramount before initiating any statistical validation or experimental diagnostic. The dataset is a massive amalgamation of three distinct distributions, totaling 7,502,559 rows and occupying approximately 5.63 gigabytes of storage in Parquet format.7

### **Constituent Data Distributions and Domain Characteristics**

The corpus is not monolithic; rather, it is a concatenated multi-domain benchmark that spans high-level algorithmic problem solving, massive multi-language competitive programming, and highly specialized, low-level GPU kernel profiling.7  
The first subset, termed APPS within the schema, originates from the established "Measuring Coding Challenge Competence With APPS" benchmark.7 Within the context of the Code-Regression dataset, it consists of 98,932 instances.7 The input strings consist primarily of Python source code implementations of competitive programming solutions. The primary target metric, captured during the authors' custom hardware profiling, is memory footprint. Specifically, the authors isolated Python-heap usage, recording it via the tracemalloc library as dyn\_peak\_alloc\_bytes.1 This subset evaluates a regression model's innate capacity to understand algorithmic space complexity natively from Python syntax. For instance, the authors document specific profiling scenarios where an ![][image8] memory solution utilizing a single counter loop consumes 5,608 bytes, whereas a less memory-efficient ![][image9] solution utilizing auxiliary caching arrays consumes 7,136 bytes.1 The ability of a model to differentiate between these two syntactical approaches and predict the resulting memory delta is the core objective of the APPS subset.  
The second and overwhelmingly largest subset is CDSS, originating from IBM's "Project CodeNet" repository.7 This subset comprises 7,391,012 rows, representing the vast majority of the dataset's total volume.7 Project CodeNet is renowned in the machine learning literature for its sheer scale and language diversity, containing algorithmic submissions across multiple programming languages, most notably Python, C++, and Java.14 The code samples in this distribution are labeled with physical CPU run time and memory footprint data.13 The immense volume of this specific subset dictates that any global statistical aggregation performed on the overall dataset will be heavily biased toward the structural characteristics of the CDSS distribution.7  
The third subset, KBSS (KernelBook), is the smallest in volume but arguably the most syntactically complex. Originating from the KernelBook repository, this subset contains 12,615 rows of low-level code.7 The input strings represent Triton GPU kernels—highly specialized, Python-like code used to write efficient custom operations for deep learning accelerators, such as custom convolution layers or flash-attention mechanisms.16 Unlike APPS and CDSS, which target memory allocations, the target metric for the KBSS subset is execution latency, measured strictly in milliseconds.6 Predicting hardware latency from Triton source code requires an implicit understanding of complex GPU memory hierarchies, thread blocking, loop unrolling, and hardware-specific compilation artifacts.18 The inclusion of this subset tests a model's ability to map high-level text representations to low-level silicon execution dynamics.

### **Schema Architecture and Structural Anomaly Analysis**

The overarching schema of the Code-Regression dataset exhibits a highly specific, standardized format explicitly designed to facilitate unified sequence-to-sequence training. A thorough audit of the schema reveals critical aliases, nomenclature inconsistencies, and structural quirks that must absolutely dictate the parameters of any downstream data processing or classical modeling efforts.7  
The table below delineates the canonical schema of the dataset, mapping the physical column structures to their operative definitions:

| Column Name | Data Type | Structural Purpose and Content Analysis |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| identifier | String | A unique alphanumeric key for the row, explicitly indicating the source space partition (e.g., APPS\_0, KBSS\_12, CDSS\_424). |
| space | String | The logical partition indicating the origin of the data (APPS, KBSS, or CDSS). |
| input | String | The raw text representation of the source code. It is internally aliased in documentation as shortest\_onnx despite containing Triton or Python source code. |
| target\_metric | String | A literal string column that consistently contains the static text value val\_accuracy across all 7.5 million rows. It serves as a legacy placeholder. |
| val\_accuracy | Float / Null | The actual continuous numeric regression target. Despite the column name indicating classification accuracy, this field actually contains continuous physical metrics like memory bytes or latency milliseconds. |
| metric\_type | String | The auxiliary label explicitly indicating what the val\_accuracy number actually represents in physical units (e.g., memory\_bytes for APPS/CDSS; latency\_ms for KBSS). |
| metadata | String | A stringified Python dictionary containing heterogeneous, source-specific execution trace data, hardware profiling parameters, and secondary execution metrics. |

The most critical and potentially disastrous anomaly in this schema for an uninformed practitioner is the extreme overloading of the val\_accuracy nomenclature. As explicitly documented in the dataset's repository schema, the column named target\_metric is statically populated with the string 'val\_accuracy', and the numeric continuous target is stored entirely within the val\_accuracy column.7 However, the values contained therein practically never represent classical model accuracy; instead, they represent continuous physical metrics like memory consumption in bytes and execution latency in milliseconds, determined entirely by the corresponding value in the metric\_type column. Researchers engaging with the raw Parquet files must apply strict conditional masking based on the metric\_type variable to prevent the catastrophic mixing of physical units (e.g., calculating the mean variance of bytes combined with milliseconds) during any foundational statistical analysis.7  
Furthermore, the metadata column is dynamically structured and highly heterogeneous depending on the space partition. For the CDSS subset, it contains a vast array of telemetry including keys for {s\_id, p\_id, u\_id, date, language, original\_language, filename\_ext, status, cpu\_time, memory, code\_size}.7 For the KBSS subset, it isolates specific profiling variances, specifically outputting the standard deviation of the latency measurements in the format {'stddev\_ms': \<value\>}.7 The text is formatted in a raw Python string syntax such that it must be parsed using Python's ast.literal\_eval library function to be safely reconstructed into a usable dictionary object.7

## **Non-LM Experimental Framework for Data Suitability Verification**

For an enterprise practitioner, statistician, or researcher seeking to understand the validity, structural integrity, and statistical viability of the akhauriyash/Code-Regression dataset *without* incurring the immense computational overhead and infrastructural complexity of training or inferencing a transformer-based language model, classical data science methodologies must be employed. The overarching goal of these experiments is to definitively prove that a latent, statistically extractable signal exists mapping the input source code strings to the val\_accuracy target metrics, entirely independent of the RLM architecture. The following experimental blueprint details the exact procedures, statistical tests, and machine learning configurations required to thoroughly validate the data.

### **Experiment 1: Distributional Diagnostics and Outlier Normalization Verification**

The most fundamental validation step involves auditing the raw physical target metrics to confirm that the execution telemetry was successfully captured, conforms to expected laws of computational complexity, and hasn't been corrupted by the val\_accuracy alias overloading present in the schema.  
**Objective:** Isolate the continuous metrics by their respective domain spaces, mathematically assess the shape of their distributions, calculate higher-order variance parameters, and empirically determine the necessity of the quantile transformations utilized in the paper.  
**Execution Protocol:**

1. Extract the raw Parquet files utilizing a highly optimized dataframe processing library, such as Polars or Apache Arrow.  
2. Apply strict conditional boolean masking to partition the master dataframe into three mutually exclusive subsets based strictly on the space identifier (APPS, KBSS, CDSS).7  
3. Execute validation assertions to ensure data purity: for the KBSS partition, assert that the metric\_type column strictly equals latency\_ms. For the APPS and CDSS partitions, assert that the column strictly equals memory\_bytes.7  
4. Compute the core descriptive statistics (mean, median, variance, standard deviation) and higher-order moments (skewness, and kurtosis) for the val\_accuracy column within each isolated partition.  
5. Apply formal normality tests, such as the Shapiro-Wilk test or the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, to mathematically quantify the deviation from a normal distribution.  
6. Generate a Kernel Density Estimate (KDE) continuous plot for the raw metrics. The APPS data, representing peak Python memory usage (dyn\_peak\_alloc\_bytes), should visually exhibit a severe positive skew with a long, heavy tail due to inefficient ![][image10] algorithms consuming massive arrays.1  
7. Apply a standard z-score standardization (![][image11]) to the target column and plot the resulting distribution.  
8. Subsequently, apply a uniform Quantile Transformation, mapping the data distribution strictly to a standard Gaussian distribution (![][image12]).  
9. **Verification Criterion:** By mathematically comparing the variance of the z-score array to the quantile array, one can independently verify the paper's critical assertion that standard z-scores fail to handle the extreme outliers, and that quantile normalization is strictly required to suppress the heavy-tailed extremes inherent to physical performance metrics.10

### **Experiment 2: Lexical, Structural, and Metadata Correlation Baselines**

Before applying any machine learning, one must prove that basic source code complexity metrics correlate with the observed physical execution metrics. Furthermore, the metadata column contains ground-truth contextual data that provides a vital secondary mechanism to verify the physical logic of the val\_accuracy targets.  
**Objective:** Unpack the stringified telemetry dictionaries, extract structural code features, and compute correlation matrices between auxiliary metadata telemetry, structural complexity, and the primary regression target to prove the dataset is physically coherent.  
**Execution Protocol:**

1. Isolate the CDSS (CodeNet) portion of the dataset, as it provides the most diverse linguistic features.  
2. Utilize Python's ast.literal\_eval function to safely parse the metadata string into an operative dictionary object for every single row.7  
3. Extract the cpu\_time, code\_size, and status keys into newly instantiated dataframe columns.7  
4. Filter out any rows where the status indicates a systemic failure (e.g., Compilation Error, Time Limit Exceeded, Memory Limit Exceeded) to ensure only valid, successfully executed source codes are analyzed.  
5. Compute the physical code size in bytes, the number of discrete lines of code (LOC), and calculate basic Halstead complexity measures (e.g., vocabulary size, program length) by parsing the raw input string.  
6. Compute the Pearson correlation coefficient (![][image13]) and the Spearman rank correlation coefficient (![][image5]) between the newly extracted cpu\_time, the computed LOC, and the primary val\_accuracy column (which functionally represents memory\_bytes for this partition).  
7. **Verification Criterion:** A definitive, positive correlation should naturally exist between algorithmic time complexity (cpu\_time), code verbosity (code\_size), and spatial complexity (memory\_bytes) within the CodeNet algorithmic corpus. Proving this multi-variable correlation independently validates that the underlying data collection and hardware profiling pipeline accurately captured cohesive, intertwined physical dynamics.13

### **Experiment 3: Signal Verification via Classical XGBoost Tabular Regression**

To definitively prove that the data holds a highly valid, extractable regression signal without relying on a transformer or any LLM architecture, the source code text must be cleanly featurized into a tabular matrix and evaluated using classical gradient-boosted decision trees. This establishes an absolute baseline noise floor for the dataset.  
**Objective:** Achieve a statistically significant Spearman rank correlation utilizing shallow machine learning, mathematically proving the target metric is inherently predictable from the syntax and structure of the source code.  
**Execution Protocol:**

1. Select a heavily stratified random sample of 250,000 rows from the CDSS (CodeNet) partition to ensure computational feasibility while maintaining statistical power.  
2. Transform the raw unstructured input strings into a massive, sparse tabular matrix utilizing Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF) vectorization. Specifically, configure the vectorizer to capture character n-grams, unigrams, and bigrams to accurately represent language syntax density (e.g., capturing the frequency of keywords like append, malloc, new, or List).1  
3. Alternatively, utilize a lightweight Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) parser (e.g., Python's native ast module for Python-specific rows) to extract deep structural features such as the maximum depth of nested for loops, the total count of variable instantiations, and the frequency of floating-point arithmetic operations, appending these as numerical columns to the feature matrix.  
4. Train an advanced XGBoost or LightGBM regression model on this sparse feature matrix, utilizing a strict 80/20 train-test split. The objective loss function must be set to minimize the pseudo-Huber loss rather than standard MSE, maintaining gradient robustness against the heavy-tailed memory targets.  
5. Generate predictions on the isolated test set and calculate both the Spearman rank correlation coefficient (![][image5]) and the Kendall-Tau (![][image7]) against the actual val\_accuracy physical values.  
6. **Verification Criterion:** Existing literature analyzing the Project CodeNet corpus demonstrates that classical models like XGBoost can accurately predict CPU time and memory consumption based purely on engineered structural features, frequently outperforming Decision Trees and LightGBM.24 If the XGBoost model pipeline achieves a moderate, statistically significant positive Spearman correlation (e.g., ![][image14] to ![][image15]), it incontrovertibly proves that the Code-Regression dataset possesses a valid, learnable signal linking lexical syntax to physical performance. This successfully validates the core efficacy of the dataset entirely independent of the RLM neural architecture.

### **Experiment 4: Information-Theoretic Context Truncation Analysis**

The previous theoretical critique highlighted the RLM's severe vulnerability to sequence token truncation limits. The dataset must be empirically audited to quantify exactly what percentage of the corpus violates the standard LLM context windows, and how much signal is lost when truncation occurs.  
**Objective:** Compute the statistical distribution of input code sequence lengths to mathematically quantify the risk of signal loss via standard truncation.  
**Execution Protocol:**

1. Initialize a standard, lightweight heuristic text tokenizer. Since an LLM is not being instantiated, a simple word-boundary regular expression tokenizer or a byte-pair encoding (BPE) simulator (such as the tiktoken library, utilizing the cl100k\_base encoding) is sufficient to accurately simulate transformer token boundaries.  
2. Apply the simulated tokenizer to the input column across all three partitions (APPS, CDSS, KBSS) to calculate the exact discrete token length of every single source code string in the dataset.  
3. Compute the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of the resulting token lengths.  
4. Establish absolute vertical threshold markers on the CDF plot at 2048 tokens, 4096 tokens, and 8192 tokens—representing the standard maximal input lengths for small-scale encoder models like T5Gemma and standard frontier models.7  
5. **Verification Criterion:** Calculate the exact fractional percentage of rows in the CDSS and APPS corpora that exceed the 2048-token threshold. If a statistically significant portion of the data (e.g., ![][image16]) lies strictly beyond this operational boundary, it provides empirical mathematical proof that the text-to-text regression paradigm will inherently experience forced data attrition. This validates the theoretical critique regarding structural truncation, proving that predicting performance from massive codebases requires alternative architectural approaches capable of infinite or highly compressed context tracking.8

## **Advanced Diagnostics: Triton Latency and Profiling Variance**

While memory footprint (APPS, CDSS) is a relatively deterministic metric based on the source code's algorithmic complexity, the KBSS subset relies on predicting hardware latency for Triton kernels. Hardware latency is notoriously non-deterministic, subject to thermal throttling, clock speed fluctuations, and background operating system interrupts. The dataset's validity heavily relies on the stability of this metric.  
To validate the KBSS dataset independently, an analyst must extract the stddev\_ms metric from the stringified metadata column for all 12,615 Triton rows.7 By dividing the standard deviation by the primary latency\_ms target (housed in the val\_accuracy column), the analyst can calculate the Coefficient of Variation (![][image17]) for the execution latency of every single kernel.  
If the calculated CV across the KBSS partition is excessively high (e.g., ![][image18]), it reveals that there is massive, inherent profiling noise in the Triton kernel executions. The paper's authors explicitly acknowledged the "typical noise levels in regression evaluation" and variance of low-level latency profiling during the peer review.4 Validating this CV establishes a theoretical upper bound on any model's predictive accuracy; if the hardware execution itself varies by ![][image19] between runs of the identical code, no regression model—whether a massive LLM or a simple XGBoost tree—can mathematically achieve an error rate lower than the underlying physical variance of the hardware.4
